rationale:
Evidence: all 60 trials in each development design so far ended off track at max_error about 0.06 m, the off-track limit, with rms_error about 0.03 m. The best design is iteration 5 (score 137.76), which has body 0.14 x 0.10, mass 0.5 kg, and sensors at y=0.07 with x=-0.06..+0.06 and a 16 mm footprint.

Two results point away from the controller gains. Iterations 2 and 4 scored identically (132.0028) although kp moved 3.0 to 2.8 and kd moved 0.4 to 1.0. Iteration 6 added ki=1.0 to iteration 5 and every metric matched to four decimals, so the integral term had no measurable effect. The bias-cancelling hypothesis from iteration 6 is therefore not supported, and I will set ki back to 0 to avoid unneeded windup.

The untested lever is turning authority. Yaw rate is roughly (right wheel minus left wheel speed) divided by wheel_track, so a narrower track gives more heading change per unit of PWM difference. Iteration 5 lowered yaw inertia, but the robot still drifts to the edge on curves. Changes: (1) wheel_track from 0.12 to 0.10 m, to increase yaw response per unit of steering command; (2) ki from 1.0 to 0, since it had no effect; (3) keep the iteration-5 geometry otherwise, and keep kp 3.0, kd 0.4, base_speed 1.3 and last_direction line loss, so the wheel-track change is isolated. Expected result: the robot corrects faster on curves, max_error stays below the limit for longer, and progress rises above the 0.55 seen on the oval. Finishing within 3 s still needs a later speed increase. If this does not move progress, the next test is base_speed toward 1.6 with wheel_track held at the new value.
